claims.text: Conventional stainless steel is passivated by a native chromium oxide layer.
Native stainless-steel passivation provides inadequate protection under extreme high-temperature and chemically aggressive conditions.
An Al-Cr-Si-rich alloy can be deposited onto stainless steel by laser cladding.
Laser cladding an Al-Cr-Si-rich alloy onto stainless steel improves corrosion resistance in extreme environments.
Native stainless-steel passivation degrades in aggressive oxidizing atmospheres or high-temperature molten salts.
The cladded layer forms a dense and continuous oxide film during high-temperature exposure.
The oxide film formed on the cladded layer is mechanically well-adherent.
The protective oxide film consists primarily of alumina and chromia.
The Al-Cr-Si composition promotes formation of a stable, protective oxide film during high-temperature oxidation.
The protective oxide film impedes diffusion of corrosive species into the stainless-steel substrate.
Rapid solidification during laser cladding refines the microstructure of the modified layer.
Laser-cladding-induced microstructural refinement can reduce defects and corrosion pathways.
The cladded stainless steel will exhibit lower mass loss than unmodified stainless steel under extreme corrosive exposure.
The cladded stainless steel will exhibit lower electrochemical corrosion rates than unmodified stainless steel.
Thermal stresses or mechanical mismatch can cause coating spallation or delamination during cyclic exposure.
Related high-performance alloy systems show improved high-temperature oxidation resistance when appropriate amounts of Al, Cr, and Si are added.
The magnitude and long-term stability of the proposed improvement on stainless steel remain uncertain and require experimental validation.
